chapter.name: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
chapter.blurb: Explores what people across India eat and how cooking practices have changed over time, the components of food (carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, minerals, roughage and water) and the deficiency diseases their lack causes, simple tests for starch, fat and protein, what makes a diet balanced versus junk food, and the value of millets and reducing food miles from farm to plate.

scope_in.item: Food choices vary across India's regions, linked to locally grown crops (Punjab, Karnataka and Manipur as worked examples in Table 3.2)
How cooking and grinding practices have changed over time (chulha to gas stove, sil-batta to electric grinder) and the reasons given for this change
Carbohydrates and fats as energy-giving foods: their sources, and fat as a stored energy source
Proteins as body-building foods and their plant and animal sources

Vitamins and minerals as protective nutrients: their functions, sources and the deficiency diseases/disorders they cause (scurvy, beriberi, rickets, night blindness/loss of vision, bone and tooth decay, goitre, anaemia), including the sailors' scurvy case and the Himalayan-region goitre/iodised-salt case
Dietary fibre (roughage) and water as essential, non-nutrient components of food, and the effect of cooking/washing on some vitamins
Simple tests to detect starch (iodine solution turning blue-black), fat (oily, light-transmitting patch on paper) and protein (copper sulfate and caustic soda solutions turning violet) in food items
Balanced diet: how nutrient requirements vary by age, gender, activity and health, and comparing packaged-food nutrition labels to identify junk food
Millets (jowar, bajra, ragi, sanwa) as nutrient-rich, easily cultivated native cereals called nutri-cereals
Food miles: the farm-to-plate journey of food and why reducing this distance matters

scope_out.item: The opening Sanskrit/Hindi verse ('annena jatani jivanti') and its translation
scope_out.reason: A decorative epigraph introducing the chapter's theme, not itself a testable science fact

scope_out.item: All 'More to know!' boxes (polar bear fat and hibernation p.41; edible mushrooms as a protein source p.42; the Agariyas' salt farming p.43; food fortification and FSSAI p.53) and the 'Know a scientist' box on Coluthur Gopalan (p.47)
scope_out.reason: The book's own front matter (fecu1ps, 'About the Book') states these box items, including scientist biographies, are explicitly non-evaluative add-on content

scope_out.item: Personal/open-ended activities that call for the student's own data (Activity 3.1's weekly food log; Activity 3.3's interviews with elderly people; Activity 3.4's neighbourhood survey; Activity 3.8's check of one's own diet; the blank Table 3.3 results template)
scope_out.reason: These require the student's own field data or personal record, with no single fixed correct answer to test against

scope_out.item: The 'Learning further' section (reading fortified-food labels, researching the Apatani tribe's tapyo salt, researching wild food varieties like ranbhajis, writing a letter to the principal about junk food, preparing a diet chart)
scope_out.reason: The book's own front matter describes 'Learning further' as a non-evaluative extension/project section

scope_out.item: The chemical-safety precautions listed for the protein test (p.49)
scope_out.reason: Lab safety instructions for conducting the activity, not conceptual science content to be tested

scope_out.item: Activity 3.2's open invitation for students to research and add further states beyond the three worked examples (Punjab, Karnataka, Manipur) given in Table 3.2
scope_out.reason: Data for other states is not provided in the book and would need independent research, so it is not fixed source content

concepts.name: Food diversity across India and changing cooking practices
concepts.description: People across India eat different traditional foods depending on locally grown crops, climate, culture and tradition, and cooking tools have changed over time.
concepts.idea: Traditional food in a region is shaped by the crops grown there, and cooking and grinding tools have moved from chulha and sil-batta to gas stoves and electric grinders.
concepts.rule: Table 3.2 gives three worked examples: Punjab (maize, wheat, chickpea, pulses) eats makki di roti, sarson da saag, chhole bhature, parantha, halwa, kheer, and drinks lassi, chhach, milk, tea; Karnataka (rice, ragi, urad, coconut) eats idli, dosa, sambhar, coconut chutney, ragi mudde, palya, rasam, rice, and drinks buttermilk, coffee, tea; Manipur (rice, bamboo, soya bean) eats rice, eromba, utti, singju, kangsoi, and drinks black tea. Cooking practices have changed from the chulha to the modern gas stove, and from the sil-batta to the electrical grinder, due to technological development, improved transportation and better communication.
concepts.example: Punjab's makki di roti and sarson da saag use maize and mustard grown locally in that region.

questions.q: Explain, using examples from the chapter, how climate and locally grown crops together shape a state's traditional diet.
questions.a: Crops that grow well in a region's soil and climate become the basis of its traditional food; for example, Punjab's wheat and maize give rise to parantha and makki di roti, while Karnataka's rice and coconut give rise to idli, dosa and coconut chutney. Traditional food therefore reflects what a region's climate and soil allow to be grown.

questions.q: Compare the traditional beverages listed for Punjab and Karnataka in Table 3.2.

questions.q: A shopkeeper claims that because idli and dosa are eaten in many parts of India, food habits do not really vary by region. Using the chapter's content, analyse whether this claim is well supported.
questions.a: The claim is not well supported. A few widely eaten dishes do not erase this regional diversity.
s: States claim is not well supported

questions.q: Do you think it is a good idea for a family to eat mostly locally grown, traditional food rather than food brought in from far away? Give one reason for your view.
questions.a: A reasoned answer either way is acceptable, for example: yes, because locally grown food suits the local climate and connects to tradition; a justified reason must be given.

questions.q: Design a short survey of three questions you could use to find out how a friend's family's food habits differ from your own, in the spirit of Activity 3.2 in the chapter.
questions.a: Any three reasonable survey questions are acceptable, for example: What crops are grown in your family's native region? What traditional dishes does your family cook often? Has your family's cooking changed since your grandparents' time?

concepts.name: Carbohydrates and fats: energy-giving foods
concepts.description: Carbohydrates and fats are the body's main energy-giving nutrients, from cereals, fruits and vegetables, and from nuts, seeds and oils.
concepts.idea: Carbohydrates provide quick energy and fats provide stored energy; together they are called energy-giving foods.
concepts.rule: Glucose, an example of a carbohydrate, provides instant energy, which is why marathon runners drink glucose water. Cereals such as wheat, rice, maize and bajra, vegetables such as potato and sweet potato, and fruits such as banana, pineapple, mango and sugarcane, as well as common sugar, are sources of carbohydrates. Ghee and oils, and nuts such as groundnut, walnut, coconut and almond, and seeds such as pumpkin and sunflower seeds, are sources of fat; fat is a source of stored energy, which is why laddoos rich in ghee and nuts are traditionally eaten in winter to keep the body warm.
concepts.example: A marathon runner drinks glucose water for instant energy from carbohydrate.

questions.a: glucose water

questions.a: energy

questions.a: groundnut

questions.a: walnut

questions.a: because it belongs to the same food component group as starchy foods

questions.a: fat

questions.q: A school lunch has only boiled rice and potato, with no nuts, oil or ghee. Explain which energy-giving food component is missing or low, and suggest one food item to add to fix this.
questions.a: Rice and potato mainly supply carbohydrate but very little fat. Adding a fat source such as a small amount of oil, ghee, nuts or seeds would supply the missing energy-giving component.

questions.q: Consider: (I) Glucose is an example of a carbohydrate. (II) Groundnuts are a source of fat, not carbohydrate. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: Compare potato and coconut as sources of energy-giving food components, based on the chapter.
questions.a: Potato is a source of carbohydrate, while coconut is a source of fat; both are energy-giving foods but supply different components.

questions.q: A student says, 'Since both carbohydrates and fats give energy, it does not matter which one I eat more of.' Analyse this statement using ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: This is not fully correct. While both are energy-giving, carbohydrates are commonly used for quick energy and fats act as a stored energy source, so they play different roles; relying too heavily on one, especially fat, is not the same as taking a balanced intake of both alongside the body's other nutrient needs.
s: Identifies both are energy-giving but play different roles
Notes carbohydrate vs fat role difference

questions.q: Do you agree that a diet with only carbohydrates and fats and no other nutrients would keep a person perfectly healthy? Justify your view.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is acceptable, for example: no, because the chapter shows the body also needs proteins, vitamins, minerals, roughage and water, so energy-giving foods alone are not enough for a balanced diet.

questions.q: Plan snacks for a school picnic that include at least one good carbohydrate source and one good fat source from the chapter, and explain your choice.
questions.a: Any reasonable plan is acceptable, for example: banana or boiled potato chaat for carbohydrate, and a small pack of roasted groundnuts or almonds for fat, explaining that together they supply quick and stored energy.
s: Overall reasoning ties to energy-giving role

concepts.name: Proteins, vitamins and minerals: body-building and protective nutrients
concepts.description: Proteins build and repair the body; vitamins and minerals protect it from deficiency diseases; dietary fibre and water are essential though not nutrients.
concepts.idea: Protein is a body-building nutrient from plant and animal sources; vitamins and minerals are protective nutrients whose lack causes specific deficiency diseases.
concepts.rule: Protein sources include plant sources (pulses, beans, peas, soya bean, nuts) and animal sources (milk, paneer, egg, fish, meat, chicken); protein-rich foods are called body-building foods. Case 1: sailors on long voyages developed bleeding, swollen gums (scurvy) cured by lemons and oranges, showing Vitamin C deficiency. Case 2: people in the Himalayan region and Northern plains developed neck swelling (goitre) from iodine-poor soil, relieved by iodised salt. The chapter's chart (Fig. 3.5) gives: Vitamin A (papaya, carrot, mango, milk) deficiency causes loss of vision/night blindness; Vitamin B1 (legumes, nuts, whole grains, milk products) deficiency causes beriberi (swelling, tingling/burning in feet and hands, breathing trouble); Vitamin C (amla, guava, green chilli, orange, lemon) deficiency causes scurvy (bleeding gums, slow wound healing); Vitamin D (sunlight, milk, butter, fish, eggs) deficiency causes rickets (soft, bent bones); Calcium (milk, curd, cheese, paneer) deficiency causes bone and tooth decay; Iodine (seaweed, water chestnut, iodised salt) deficiency causes goitre; Iron (green leafy vegetables, beetroot, pomegranate) deficiency causes anaemia (weakness, shortness of breath). Vitamins and minerals together are called protective nutrients, needed in small amounts; some vitamins like Vitamin C can be lost during cooking or washing. Dietary fibre (roughage), from plant products such as green leafy vegetables, fruits, whole grains, pulses and nuts, gives no nutrients but helps remove undigested food and ensures smooth passage of stools. Water helps the body absorb nutrients and removes waste through sweat and urine.
concepts.example: Sailors on long voyages who ate lemons and oranges recovered from scurvy, caused by Vitamin C deficiency.

questions.a: protein

questions.q: A person eats plenty of pulses, milk and paneer but no meat or fish. Based on the chapter, this diet still contains a protein source because

o: milk products and pulses are also good sources of protein

questions.q: Gourav's doctor gave him calcium tablets after his leg fracture, and Vitamin D syrup along with calcium on his second visit. Using the chapter's chart, explain why both were needed together.
questions.a: Calcium keeps bones and teeth healthy and is needed to help repair the fractured bone, but the body needs Vitamin D to properly absorb calcium. Giving Vitamin D along with calcium ensures the calcium is actually taken up and used by the body.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Fruits and vegetables should ideally be eaten raw or lightly cooked. Reason (R): Some nutrients like Vitamin C can be lost during cooking due to high heat. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.q: Compare the deficiency diseases caused by a lack of iodine and a lack of iron, as described in the chapter.
questions.a: Iodine deficiency causes goitre, seen as swelling at the front of the neck; iron deficiency causes anaemia, with symptoms of weakness and shortness of breath. Both are mineral deficiencies but affect the body differently.

questions.q: A student argues that since vitamins and minerals are needed only 'in small amounts', they are less important than carbohydrates and fats. Analyse whether the chapter supports this view.
questions.a: The chapter does not support this view. Although vitamins and minerals are needed in smaller quantities than carbohydrates and fats, they are essential for protecting the body from serious deficiency diseases like scurvy, goitre, rickets and anaemia. A small requirement does not mean low importance.
s: States the view is not well supported
Notes small quantity does not mean unimportant

questions.q: A friend says fortified foods like iodised salt are unnecessary if a person eats a balanced diet. Do you agree? Justify using ideas about iodine deficiency from the chapter.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is acceptable, for example: iodised salt remains a useful safeguard because iodine-poor soil in some regions can mean even a generally balanced diet does not supply enough iodine, as shown by the goitre cases in the chapter.

questions.q: Design a one-day sample menu for a child who currently gets almost no Vitamin C or iron in her diet, using foods named in the chapter, and explain your choices.
questions.a: Any reasonable menu using named foods is acceptable, for example: include amla or orange for Vitamin C and green leafy vegetables or beetroot for iron, explaining that these directly address the two deficiencies.
s: Vitamin C food chosen and justified
Explanation ties choices to preventing deficiency

concepts.name: Testing food for starch, fat and protein
concepts.description: Simple lab tests can detect starch, fat and protein in food using iodine solution, a paper-and-light method, and copper sulfate with caustic soda.
concepts.idea: A blue-black colour with iodine solution shows starch, an oily light-transmitting patch on paper shows fat, and a violet colour with copper sulfate and caustic soda shows protein.
concepts.rule: Starch test: add 2-3 drops of diluted iodine solution to the food item; a blue-black colour indicates starch. Fat test: wrap the food item in paper, press it, let it dry if needed, then hold it to light; an oily patch through which light shines faintly indicates fat. Protein test: make a paste of the food item, put it in a test tube with water, add copper sulfate solution and then caustic soda solution, and shake; a violet colour indicates protein. Peanuts test positive for both protein and fat, showing a food can contain more than one nutrient. Sugar does not turn blue-black with iodine even though it is a carbohydrate, because the iodine test specifically detects starch.
concepts.example: A slice of potato turns blue-black when tested with iodine solution, showing it contains starch.

questions.q: Which solution is used to test a food item for the presence of starch?
questions.a: iodine solution

questions.q: A blue-black colour after adding iodine solution to a food item indicates the presence of ____.
questions.a: starch

questions.q: An oily patch on paper that lets light shine faintly through it indicates the presence of
questions.a: fat

questions.a: to check whether it leaves an oily patch on the paper
o: to check whether it leaves an oily patch on the paper
to change its colour with iodine

questions.q: A violet colour after adding copper sulfate and caustic soda solutions indicates the presence of ____.
questions.a: protein

questions.q: Why must the paper be allowed to dry before checking for an oily patch, if the food item contains a little water?
questions.a: so that water does not get mistaken for an oily patch
o: so that water does not get mistaken for an oily patch
so that the paper turns blue-black
so that the food loses its starch
so that the iodine solution works better

questions.q: Why does the chapter find that peanuts test positive for both protein and fat?
questions.a: because a single food item can contain more than one nutrient
o: because a single food item can contain more than one nutrient
because peanuts are tested with iodine only
because fat and protein are the same nutrient

questions.q: Describe what colour change to look for in the starch test and what it indicates.
questions.a: Watch for the food item's colour to turn blue-black after adding iodine solution; this blue-black colour indicates the presence of starch.

questions.q: A boiled potato turns blue-black when a drop of iodine solution is added to it. This shows the potato contains
questions.a: starch

questions.q: A piece of butter wrapped in paper leaves a clear oily patch that light shines through. This shows butter contains
questions.a: fat

questions.q: A student tests boiled gram with copper sulfate and caustic soda solutions and sees the mixture turn violet. This result means the boiled gram contains
questions.a: protein

questions.q: A student presses a piece of cucumber in paper and sees no oily patch, but the cucumber turns blue-black with iodine solution. What can she conclude about cucumber's starch and fat content?
questions.a: Cucumber tested positive for starch, shown by the blue-black colour, but negative for fat, shown by the absence of an oily patch.

questions.q: Sugar does not turn blue-black when tested with iodine solution, even though it is a carbohydrate. What does this suggest?
questions.a: the iodine test detects starch specifically, not all carbohydrates
o: the iodine test detects starch specifically, not all carbohydrates
sugar contains no carbohydrate at all
the iodine test detects any carbohydrate equally

questions.q: A few drops of iodine solution fell on Mishti's socks and on her teacher's cotton saree. The saree turned blue-black but the socks did not change colour. Explain a possible reason for this difference, using ideas from the starch test.
questions.a: A blue-black colour with iodine indicates starch. The saree's cotton fabric likely had starch present in it, perhaps from starching or finishing the cloth, while the material of the socks had no starch present, so only the saree changed colour.
s: Explains saree changed because starch was present
Explains socks did not change because no starch was present

questions.q: Consider: (I) A blue-black colour with iodine solution indicates starch. (II) A violet colour after adding copper sulfate and caustic soda indicates fat. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Compare the visible result of a positive starch test and a positive protein test.
questions.a: A positive starch test shows a blue-black colour after adding iodine solution, while a positive protein test shows a violet colour after adding copper sulfate and caustic soda solutions.

questions.q: A student claims that if a food item does not turn blue-black with iodine, it must contain no carbohydrate at all. Analyse this claim using the chapter's discussion of sugar.
questions.a: The claim is incorrect. Sugar is a carbohydrate but does not turn blue-black with iodine, because the iodine test specifically detects starch, not all carbohydrates. A negative iodine test only rules out starch, not every carbohydrate.
s: Explains the test is starch-specific, not for all carbohydrates

questions.q: A student wants to check whether an unknown liquid could be iodine solution. Suggest a simple check she could do, and justify it using what a positive starch test looks like.
questions.a: She could add the liquid to a known starchy food such as a piece of potato or rice; if it is iodine solution, the food would turn blue-black, confirming its identity.
s: Suggests testing on a starchy food
Justifies using the blue-black colour change

questions.q: Design a short experiment, listing the steps, to find out whether a slice of bread contains starch, fat and protein, using the three tests described in the chapter.
questions.a: Any reasonable plan following the book's three tests is acceptable, for example: (1) add drops of iodine solution to a piece of bread and check for a blue-black colour for starch; (2) press another piece of bread in paper and hold it to light to check for an oily patch for fat; (3) make a paste of bread in water, add copper sulfate then caustic soda solution and check for a violet colour for protein.

concepts.name: Balanced diet and junk food
concepts.description: Nutrient needs vary from person to person; a balanced diet supplies all nutrients, roughage and water in the right amounts, while junk food is high in sugar and fat but low in other nutrients.
concepts.idea: A balanced diet meets an individual's nutrient needs, which vary by age, gender, activity and health, while junk food is high-calorie but nutrient-poor.
concepts.rule: A diet that has all essential nutrients, roughage and water in the right amount for proper growth and development is a balanced diet. Nutrient requirements vary according to age, gender, physical activity, health status and lifestyle. Comparing nutrition labels (per 100 g: potato wafers 536 kcal, 35.0 g fat, 53.0 g carbohydrate, 7.0 g protein, 4.8 g dietary fibre; roasted chana 355 kcal, 6.26 g fat, 58.58 g carbohydrate, 18.64 g protein, 16.8 g dietary fibre) shows wafers are high in fat and calories but low in protein and fibre, the definition of junk food. Junk foods include potato wafers, candy bars and carbonated drinks; frequent consumption is linked to obesity and other health problems.
concepts.example: Comparing the nutrition labels of potato wafers and roasted chana shows wafers are much higher in fat and calories but much lower in protein and fibre.

questions.q: A diet that has all essential nutrients, roughage and water in the right amounts for proper growth is called a
questions.a: balanced diet

questions.q: Foods high in sugar and fat but low in protein, minerals, vitamins and fibre are called ____ foods.
questions.a: junk

questions.q: Which of these is given in the chapter as an example of junk food?
questions.a: potato wafers

questions.q: A child's daily diet is mostly rice and fried snacks, with no fruit, vegetables, milk or pulses. Identify one way this diet fails to be balanced, and one change to fix it.
questions.a: Any valid answer is acceptable, for example: it lacks vitamins, minerals, protein and roughage from fruits, vegetables, pulses and milk; adding these food groups in the right amount would help make it balanced.

questions.a: because factors like gender, activity level and health status also matter, not age alone

questions.q: A parent packs her child's lunchbox with only potato wafers and a carbonated drink every day. Using the chapter's ideas, explain why this is not a balanced diet and suggest a better combination of foods for the lunchbox.
questions.a: This lunch is not a balanced diet because it is high in sugar, fat and calories but very low in protein, vitamins, minerals and fibre, matching the chapter's description of junk food. A better lunchbox would include a protein source such as paneer or pulses, a fruit or vegetable for vitamins and fibre, and a moderate carbohydrate item, instead of junk food and sugary drinks.
s: Explains why current lunch is junk-food-like/unbalanced
Suggests a protein or fibre-rich addition
Suggests a more balanced overall combination

questions.q: Assertion (A): A balanced diet is not the same for every person. Reason (R): Nutrient requirements vary with age, gender, physical activity, health status and lifestyle. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Compare potato wafers and roasted chana in terms of dietary fibre and protein content, based on the chapter's data.
questions.a: Roasted chana has much more dietary fibre, 16.8 g compared with 4.8 g per 100 g, and much more protein, 18.64 g compared with 7 g per 100 g, than potato wafers.

questions.q: A snack company advertises its potato wafers as 'a great source of energy for growing children.' Analyse whether this claim, using the chapter's data, gives the full picture of the food's suitability for a growing child's diet.
questions.a: The claim is technically true that wafers are high in energy at 536 kcal per 100 g, but it is misleading as a full recommendation. Growing children also need protein, vitamins, minerals and fibre, all of which wafers provide in very low amounts compared with a food like roasted chana, so wafers alone would make an unbalanced, junk-food-heavy diet.
s: Acknowledges the energy claim has some truth
Notes what the claim leaves out (protein/vitamins/minerals/fibre)
Concludes the claim does not describe a balanced choice

questions.q: Do you think schools should allow potato wafers and carbonated drinks to be sold in their canteens? Justify your view using ideas about junk food from the chapter.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is acceptable, for example: no, because the chapter shows such foods are high in sugar and fat and low in other nutrients, and frequent consumption can cause obesity and health problems, so schools should limit them.

questions.q: Design a one-day snack plan for a twelve-year-old that avoids junk food, using ideas about balanced diet from the chapter, and explain why each item is a good choice.
questions.a: Any reasonable plan is acceptable, for example: a fruit, roasted chana or nuts, and a glass of milk, explaining that together they supply protein, vitamins, minerals and fibre while avoiding the high sugar/fat, low-nutrient profile of junk food.
s: At least two suitable snack items chosen
Explanation notes avoidance of junk food traits

concepts.name: Millets and food miles
concepts.description: Millets are nutrient-rich, easily cultivated native Indian cereals; food miles is the distance food travels from farm to plate.
concepts.idea: Millets are called nutri-cereals for their nutritional value and easy cultivation, and reducing food miles cuts cost and pollution while keeping food fresh and supporting local farmers.
concepts.rule: Millets such as jowar, bajra, ragi and sanwa are small-sized grains native to India that can be cultivated in different climatic conditions; they are good sources of vitamins, minerals like iron and calcium, and dietary fibre, which is why they are also called nutri-cereals. Food miles is the total distance a food item travels from producer to consumer. The chapter's farm-to-plate diagram (Fig. 3.10) shows the steps: a farmer growing wheat, threshing and winnowing of grains, storage of grains, grinding of grains and packing, transport to the retail shop, and finally food on our plate. Reducing food miles cuts down cost and pollution during transport, helps support local farmers, and keeps food fresh and healthy.
concepts.example: Ragi, a millet, is a nutrient-rich nutri-cereal that can be grown in varied climatic conditions.

questions.q: Which of these is given in the chapter as an example of a millet?
questions.a: bajra

questions.q: Millets are also known as ____-cereals because of their high nutritional value.
questions.a: nutri

questions.a: because they are rich sources of vitamins, minerals like iron and calcium, and dietary fibre
o: because they are rich sources of vitamins, minerals like iron and calcium, and dietary fibre

questions.q: Which step comes first in the 'farm to plate' journey shown in the chapter's diagram?
questions.a: farmer growing wheat

questions.a: they can be cultivated in different climatic conditions
o: they can be cultivated in different climatic conditions
they grow only near the sea
they require no sunlight at all

questions.q: Name two reasons the chapter gives for why reducing food miles is important.
questions.a: Any two of: cuts down cost and pollution during transport, helps support local farmers, keeps food fresh and healthy.

questions.q: A family buys wheat grown by a nearby farmer instead of wheat transported from a very distant region. This choice would
questions.a: reduce the food's food miles
o: turn the wheat into a millet

questions.q: A child eats ragi porridge instead of a highly processed snack for breakfast. This is a good choice mainly because ragi is a
questions.a: nutrient-rich millet

questions.q: Two bags of the same grain are available: one grown 20 km away and one transported from 2000 km away. Based on the idea of food miles, which is likely to have lower food miles and why?
questions.a: the one grown 20 km away, because it travels a much shorter distance to reach the consumer
o: the one grown 20 km away, because it travels a much shorter distance to reach the consumer
the one from 2000 km away, because distance does not affect food miles
both have identical food miles regardless of distance
food miles only depend on the crop type, not distance

questions.q: List two steps, in the correct order, that come between 'farmer growing wheat' and 'food on our plate' in the chapter's farm-to-plate diagram.
questions.a: Any two of, in a sensible order: threshing and winnowing of grains, storage of grains, grinding of grains and packing, transport to retail shop.
s: Second step named in correct order

questions.q: A region has rocky, less fertile soil and unpredictable rainfall, and wants to grow a nutritious cereal crop reliably. Based on the chapter, which type of crop would suit this best?
questions.a: millets

questions.q: A city wants to reduce the food miles of its wheat supply. Using the farm-to-plate diagram in the chapter, suggest one practical change the city could make, and explain how it would reduce food miles.
questions.a: The city could source wheat from farms closer to the city instead of distant regions, or support local grinding and packing facilities rather than transporting grain long distances for processing. Either change shortens the total distance travelled from producer to consumer, reducing food miles, cost and pollution.
s: Suggests a concrete change (e.g. sourcing locally)
Explains it shortens the farm-to-plate distance
Links to reduced cost/pollution as in the chapter

questions.q: Consider: (I) Millets can be cultivated in different climatic conditions. (II) Reducing food miles helps support local farmers. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: Compare millets and highly processed packaged snacks in terms of their contribution to a nutritious, low-food-miles diet.
questions.a: Millets are nutrient-rich, being good sources of vitamins, iron, calcium and fibre, and if locally grown they travel a shorter distance, giving lower food miles. Many packaged snacks are lower in these nutrients and may travel further to reach the consumer, giving higher food miles.
s: Millets - nutrition and/or lower food miles point

questions.q: A farmer argues that growing millets instead of a water-intensive crop in a dry region makes more sense both nutritionally and environmentally. Analyse this argument using ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: The argument is well supported. Millets can be grown in varied and difficult climatic conditions unlike more demanding crops, and they are rich in vitamins, minerals and fibre. Growing them locally in a suited region also keeps food miles low, reducing cost and pollution, so the choice benefits both nutrition and the environment.
s: Links local cultivation to lower food miles/environmental benefit

questions.q: Do you think schools should encourage students to eat locally grown millets instead of imported processed cereals? Justify your view using ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is acceptable, for example: yes, because millets are nutrient-rich and, if locally grown, have lower food miles, supporting both health and local farmers.
s: Justification referencing nutrition and/or food miles

questions.q: Design a simple poster message, with two or three key points, encouraging your school community to reduce food waste and food miles, based on ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: Any reasonable set of points is acceptable, for example: take only as much food as you can eat to avoid waste; choose locally grown food and millets when possible to reduce food miles; remember the effort farmers put into growing food.
s: Point about choosing local food/millets to cut food miles
Point reflecting respect for farmers' effort or overall reasoning
